slides.theme: Headline: Weights and size. Bigger is smarter. And pricier.
slides.script: Weights, or parameters, are the numbers a model learns in training. Models get better in a predictable way with more parameters, more data and more compute. Bigger models cost more to run, so labs also make small ones, for example by distillation: training a small model to copy a big one. Open-weight models are ones you can download and run yourself. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: Headline: How a model is made. Read. Predict. Get taught manners.
slides.script: Pretraining: the model reads a huge pile of text and learns to predict the next word. Post-training teaches it to follow instructions: fine-tuning on examples, then people ranking answers (RLHF). Anthropic also uses Constitutional AI, where the model gives feedback on its own answers from a written list of principles. The training data stops at a date, the knowledge cutoff. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: Open the door: welcome, the topic in one line, and what they'll get.
slides.script:
[walk to the middle, wait for the room to settle] Hi everyone, and thanks for coming. Thanks to [meetup name] for having me.

Tonight is about how my job changed. Not so long ago I was a developer who wrote code all day. These days I'm more of an AI builder. I decide what gets built, I hand the building to AI, and I check that it's right.

I'll keep this honest. No hype, no "AI will replace us all". We'll go from what AI actually is, to how I work with it every day, to a video of me building something real. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: Howdy, I'm Erik Developer for ages. Always asking: who is this for?
slides.script: So who am I? I'm Erik. I've been a software developer for a long time. Most of it on the side closest to people. Design, frontend, the stuff people actually click on. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: Who's talking, in four short lines, ending on the shift.
slides.script:
And the questions I care about have stayed the same the whole way. Who is this for? What problem are we solving, and for whom? How will it actually be used, in the end? And how do we help people solve their problem in the most effective way?

Today I'm a consultant at Sigma Technology, placed at Teneo. There I build Teneo X, where you build, test and run your own voice and chat agents. So I work with AI in the product, and with AI to build the product.

Here's the funny part. AI took over most of the typing. Those questions? Still mine. They matter more than ever. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: Who's here? Developers. Builders. Newcomers.
slides.script: Before we ride, a quick check. [ask for a show of hands] Who here writes code most days? [pause] Nice, most of you. Keep your hand up if AI writes most of that code for you. [pause] And who hasn't really started with AI yet? Be honest, nobody's grading you. [click]

slides.theme: Find out who's in the room and make the newcomers feel welcome.
slides.script:
Good. That's pretty much the three groups on the screen. Developers, who write code and wonder what AI means for their job. Builders, who make things and want to make more, faster. And newcomers, who haven't started and maybe feel they've missed the wagon.

To the newcomers: you haven't. Honestly, starting now might even be an advantage, because you skip a lot of the clumsy early years. I'll come back to that later, I promise. [click]

slides.theme: State the core idea plainly and let it land.
slides.script:
[read slowly] I used to write the code. Now I decide what gets built, and make sure it's right. [pause]

That's the whole shift. For most of my career, a lot of my value was in my fingers. How fast I could type out a solution.

Today the typing is mostly done by AI. What's left for me is the part on either side. Before: what's the problem, and what does done look like? After: is what came back right, and good, and something I'd put my name on?

So the work didn't go away. It moved. But you can't direct something you don't understand. So let's start with what this AI thing actually is. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: What is AI, anyway? A big umbrella. LLMs are the bit everyone means.
slides.script: So, what is AI? It's a big umbrella. Any computer doing something we'd call smart. The chess computer that beat Kasparov in 1997? AI. Your spam filter? AI. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: AI is the umbrella; LLMs are what people mean today.
slides.script:
Inside that is machine learning. Instead of writing the rules yourself, you show the computer lots of examples, and it works out the rules. Inside that, deep learning: huge networks of numbers, loosely inspired by the brain.

And inside that, the thing everyone means when they say AI today. Large language models. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini. When I say AI tonight, that's what I mean. [click]
slides.change: New in the October 14 restructure.

slides.theme: Headline: It predicts the next word. That's it. Just at a huge scale.
slides.script: A large language model does one thing. It predicts the next word. [point at the sentence] The cat sat on the... mat, probably. It picks a likely word, adds it, and goes again. Word by word. That simple trick, at huge scale, turns out to write code, explain physics and plan your week. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: An LLM predicts the next word; tokens, context window, knowledge cutoff.
slides.script:
Three words worth knowing. Tokens: it reads and writes in small chunks, bits of words. The context window: its working memory, everything it can see right now. When it's full, things fall out. And the knowledge cutoff: it learned from text up to a date, and knows little after that.

How is it made? First it reads a huge pile of text and learns to predict. Then it's taught manners: follow instructions, be helpful, say no to bad requests. [click]
slides.change: New in the October 14 restructure.

slides.theme: Headline: A quarter full. 261k of 1M tokens. All re-read, every message.
slides.script: Here's what that looks like for real. This is the session where I built this deck. Partway through today, it had about two hundred and sixty thousand tokens in its window. A quarter of its working memory. Everything we'd said, every file it read, every search. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: Real numbers: this talk's prep session used about a quarter of a 1M-token window.
slides.script: And here's the part people miss. Every time I send a message, all of that gets read again. Keep that in mind. It comes back in a minute. [click]
slides.change: New Oct 14: example slide from a real session.

slides.theme: Headline: Models come in sizes. Small job, small model. Big job, strong model.
slides.script: There isn't one AI. There are models, and they come in sizes. I'll use Claude as the example, since that's what I use. Haiku is the quick hand: fast and cheap, great for simple jobs in bulk. Sonnet is the all-rounder. Opus is the workhorse, for long, hard work, like my daily coding. And Fable is the top shelf, for the hardest reasoning. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: Models come in sizes: pick by the job, and learn each one's temperament.
slides.script:
Bigger is smarter, but slower and pricier. My rule: start strong, and move down when your own tests show a cheaper one does the job.

And every model has its own temperament. Some want short, direct orders. Some do better with the whole story. You learn their quirks, like you learn a colleague's. [click]

slides.script: And this is how I actually pick. Real sessions from the last few months. Removing a risky line from my shell setup: the quick model, one minute. Deploying my shopping-list app at home: three minutes. A weather widget on my website: eleven minutes. [click]

slides.theme: Real sessions, real model choices, and what they cost.
slides.script: The big stuff goes on the strong models. A rally stage creator I built over three weeks: about thirty-seven dollars at API prices. Preparing this talk: about six dollars so far. [pause] Cheaper than the coffee I drank while doing it. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: A chat answers. An agent does the work.
slides.script: A chat answers you. An agent does the work. The difference is three things: a model, tools, and a loop. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: An agent is a model plus tools plus a loop; MCP adds tools; agents managing agents.
slides.script:
[point at the loop] It gets a goal. It thinks about the next step. It acts, using a tool: reads a file, edits code, runs a command, searches the web. It checks what happened. And it goes round again, until it's done or it needs me.

The tools are what make it useful. There's a standard plug for adding more, called MCP. Think USB-C for AI. Plug in GitHub, Figma, your calendar, and the agent can use them itself.

What changed for me recently: agents managing agents. My main session works like a manager. It splits the work and hands pieces to helper agents that each do one job and report back. Over two weeks this autumn, that was about five hundred handed-out tasks.

For the power users: one night my agents closed all sixteen issues on a list and called it done. A second check found seven not fully fixed. Now a fresh agent reviews the work, never the one that wrote it. [click]
slides.change: New in the October 14 restructure.

slides.theme: Headline: One message. One helper agent. Two minutes.
slides.script: A real one. Five in the morning, early September. My shopping-list app had a new feature, and the server at home needed updating. I sent one message. My main session handed it to a helper agent and said: I'll report back. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: The shopping-list deploy: one message, a helper agent, 21 tool calls, 2 minutes.
slides.script: Two minutes and twenty-one tool calls later, it was done. And look at what it caught on its own. The server was behind, so it fetched first. The database needed three backup files, not one. The list came back empty, so before panicking it checked the backup: it was empty before. Nothing lost. [click]
slides.change: New Oct 14: example slide from a real session.

slides.theme: Headline: It has no memory. Everything is sent again. Every single turn.
slides.script: So how do you keep an agent in check? Here's something that surprised me. The model has no memory between messages. None. Every time I hit enter, the app packs everything up and sends it again, from the top. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: No memory between messages: system prompt, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, skills, tools and the conversation are sent again every turn.
slides.script:
[point at the stack] First the system prompt: the tool's own rules, and the tools it may use. Then my rules: a file called CLAUDE.md. Other tools read one called AGENTS.md. Same idea, and one line can pull one into the other. Then the skills and tools, as one-liners. Then the whole conversation so far. And last, my new message.

That's why a rule in CLAUDE.md works. It's read again on every single turn, so the agent can't drift away from it. [point at the file] These are from mine. A pass or fail check before anything gets built. Hands off the shared database until I say the magic word. A fresh agent reviews the work, never the one that wrote it.

It's also why long sessions get slow and get summarised. The pile gets big. [click]
slides.change: New Oct 14: example slide from a real session.

slides.theme: Headline: Skills: know-how in a folder. Opened only when needed.
slides.script: If agents are the workers, skills are their know-how. A skill is a folder. Instructions in a file called SKILL.md, plus scripts or templates if the job needs them. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: A skill is know-how in a folder; only its description is always visible; it loads when a task matches.
slides.script:
[point at the file] This is a real one from my machine. It makes a report of what I've used Claude for. Look at the top. A name, and a description that says when to use it.

And that's the clever bit. The agent only keeps the name and that description in view. A few lines each. The full recipe opens only when a task matches. So you can have dozens of skills without filling up its memory. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: Said it three times? Make it a skill.
slides.script: So when is a skill worth making? My signs. I've explained the same thing three times. There's a checklist I always want followed. The output has a fixed shape, like a report or a deck. Or there's a script that should run the same way every time. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: When to make a skill, and when it should be CLAUDE.md, MCP or just a question; two ways skills run.
slides.script:
And when it's something else. A one-off? Just ask. A rule that's true for every task? That goes in CLAUDE.md. Need to reach another system? That's an MCP tool.

Two ways a skill runs. Either the agent sees that your request matches the description and loads it by itself. Or you call it by name, with a slash. [click]

Give me an update on sprint seven, typo included, and back comes the status. Eight sub-issues done, all tests green, one pull request waiting for me. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: Be clear about done. Explore. Plan. Review. Not sure? Build a demo.

slides.theme: What will always be true: explore together and review the plan; define done; not sure, build a demo and iterate.
slides.script:
[point left] One way in: explore together. Talk it through with the AI until you're on common ground. Then ask for a plan, and review it before anything gets built.

[point middle] The other: define a real goal. What is done? How will we know? The models always try to reach the goal you give them. So help them help you. The clearer you are about what you want, the better the agent performs.

[point right] And if you're not sure yet, explore some more. Make a demo, a proof of concept. It's cheap now. Try it, give feedback, adjust, iterate. Design the solution and the goal together, in a way that suits you. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: Prototype first. Use it. Then grow it.
slides.script: My shopping-list app went exactly like that. I wasn't sure what I wanted. So first, a clickable prototype on a free web page. Then a Telegram bot, so the family could add groceries for real. Three approved users. [click]

slides.theme: The shopping-list app: prototype first, real use, features from feedback, a concrete definition of done.
slides.script:
Using it told me what was missing. Feedback became features: a list API on my home server, and in September, saved carts.

And by then, done was crystal clear. Health says ok, carts is empty, my items are still there. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: Define. Direct. Judge. I own both ends. AI does the middle.
slides.script: So where's the human in all this? In the loop. This is my working loop. Three steps, and I go round it many times a day, on tasks big and small. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: Where the human sits: define, direct, judge.
slides.script:
Define. That's me. What's the problem, and how will we know it's solved? I agree on the check before anything gets built. Otherwise the AI decides when it's done, and it's very optimistic about that.

Direct. That's me and the AI together. We agree on a plan in small steps. Then the AI builds, and I steer. If it drifts off the plan, I pull it back.

Judge. That's me again. I review it with taste, I look at the proof that it works, and then it ships.

[pause] I own both ends of the loop. The AI does most of the middle. [click]
slides.change: Now sets up the video: "watch for define, direct, judge".

slides.theme: Headline: 11 minutes. Idea to live, just after midnight.
slides.script: Here's the loop on a real task. Just after midnight in September. I wanted a little weather widget on my website. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: The weather widget: define, direct, judge, in 11 minutes, with exact quotes.
slides.script:
[point at Define] Seven minutes past. My ask, typos and all. What I want, and why: a cute weather indicator, and to show I'm from Stockholm. And: plan it, interview me about it.

[point at Direct] Twelve past. It suggested an extra check. I said skip it, I'll look at it live. It opened a pull request.

[point at Judge] Seventeen past. Merge it. Then I looked, and the border was wrong. Remove it, push it straight out. Live at eighteen past. [pause] Eleven minutes, and my part was deciding. [click]

slides.theme: Headline: Plan before code. Nothing changes until I say yes.
slides.script: Here's a tool that makes define and direct concrete. It's called plan mode. [click]
slides.change: Oct 14: split into a big headline slide and a detail slide.

slides.theme: Plan mode: the AI reads the code and writes a plan, but changes nothing until I approve it. Define and direct, made concrete.
slides.script:
In plan mode the AI reads the code, looks around and writes a plan. But it doesn't touch a single file until I say yes. In Claude Code you press Shift and Tab until it says plan mode. Then you read the plan, and you can edit it before you approve.

So I see the route before we ride out. Not after.

Is it always worth it? No. It adds a step. If you could describe the change in one sentence, skip it. Use it when the change touches many files, when you're unsure how to do it, or when you don't know the code. [click]

slides.theme: Three habits of a trail boss, with one short story of being led astray.
slides.script: Iterate, don't restart. Say what's off and ask for another go. The second answer is usually better. And let it ask you questions first. End with "ask me anything you need first." It finds the gaps you missed. [click]

[point at the prompt] A quick one, on exactly the topics I need to move forward. Not a course. Not the whole history of the subject. Just enough to get unstuck, at my level. Then it checks I got it, and I'm back to work.

It's like a patient senior colleague who never sighs. No question is too basic. You can ask the same thing five times, five different ways.

And it works outside code too. Tax rules. A new framework. What someone in the meeting meant by "idempotent". [pause] The thing that used to stop you is now a ten-minute detour. [click]

slides.theme: A history lesson: the spinning jenny made spinning much faster, and people ended up working more, not less. My bet is AI goes the same way.
slides.script:
So where does this leave us? A quick history lesson. Around 1764, in England, a guy called James Hargreaves builds the spinning jenny. Before, one spinner worked one thread. Now one spinner runs eight at once. Later machines ran over a hundred.

So people worked less, right? [pause] Nope. A historian went through old court records, where witnesses mention what they were doing and when. [point at the left chart] By 1800 the working year was about a third longer than in the 1750s. By 1830, still about a fifth longer. Not longer days. Fewer days off: people stopped taking Mondays off, and the holy days disappeared.

There's a name for this pattern. The Jevons paradox. Make something cheaper to use, and we often end up using more of it. Coal back then. Thread. Now, code.

And not everyone won. [point at the right chart] In 1806 a handloom weaver earned about twice what a factory worker did. By 1820, about a quarter less.

So this isn't a law of nature. It's my bet. AI makes building software cheaper, so we'll want a lot more of it. More things to build, and I think more people building them. [click]

And imagination. Picturing what could exist that doesn't yet. [pause] And that's the catch. We can build almost anything we can imagine now. The limit isn't the code anymore. It's us. [click]

slides.theme: Thank-you and Q&A, with backup questions if the room is quiet.
slides.script:
Thank you so much. I've got about fifteen minutes for questions. Anything goes, including "that sounds terrible". [take questions; repeat each one out loud so everyone, and the recording, hears it]

[if quiet] A question I get a lot is...

Backup 1. What do I NOT use AI for? Deciding what's worth building, and the final yes or no on anything that ships. Also anything where I can't check the result, because then I can't judge it. And sometimes a two-line fix is just faster to type myself.

Backup 2. Doesn't this make juniors obsolete? I don't think so, but it changes how you learn. Juniors can ship much more, much earlier. The risk is skipping the understanding, so use AI to explain things, not just to do them. You still need to know how code works to judge it.

Backup 3. How do I check the AI's work? Same as a colleague's pull request. I agree on a check before it builds, a test or a command that says pass or fail. Then I read the diff, the list of changes, and click through the real thing. If I can't verify it, it doesn't ship.

Backup 4. What does it cost? [cost, e.g. a monthly subscription of around X per seat]. Compared to an hour of a developer's time, it pays for itself fast. Start on the cheapest plan and see if you hit the limits.

Backup 5. What about company code and privacy? Follow your company's rules first. That's not optional. Use business plans where your code isn't used for training, and never paste secrets or customer data. It's also why the video tonight used my own hobby project.

[when time's up] Thanks again. Slides and links are at [resource links], and you can reach me at [contact].

slides.theme: Make the change concrete, row by row, and reassure developers their skills still count.
slides.script:
Here's the before and after. I'll go row by row.

My main job. As a developer, I wrote the code. As an AI builder, I define the problem. Writing a clear problem turns out to be harder than writing the fix. If I can't explain it, the AI can't build it.

Where my time goes. It used to be implementing. Now it's instructing and reviewing. A lot of reading. More reading than I've done since school, honestly.

Who I work with. It used to be me and my editor. Now it's several AI agents at once, each on its own task. An agent is an AI that takes a task and works through it on its own, instead of just answering a question. Think of it as a small team that never gets tired and never gets bored, but also never pushes back unless you ask it to.

My value. It used to be how fast I build. Now it's what I choose to build, and taste. Knowing what's good and what isn't.

And what done means. It used to be: the code runs without errors. Now it's: it's verified, and it solves the actual problem. That's a higher bar, not a lower one. Code that runs but solves the wrong thing doesn't count anymore.

[pause] And to the developers in the room: none of your skills are wasted. Knowing how code works is exactly what lets me judge what the AI hands back. Without that, I'd just be nodding along.

[ask the room] Which of these rows already feels true for you? [let one or two people answer, then click]

slides.theme: Boil the new role down to three jobs and prime them to spot each one in the video.
slides.script:
If I boil the new role down, it's three jobs.

One: produce. That means deciding what problem is worth solving, and why. And owning the outcome, all the way from idea to shipped. If it breaks, it's on me, not on the AI. A lot of the time, the best call is deciding what not to build. The AI doesn't get the angry message in the morning. I do.

Two: instruct. Give the AI the context, the constraints, and a clear way to check the work. If I'd hand a new colleague a task, what would I tell them? Same thing here. The more vague I am, the more vague the result. Garbage in, very confident garbage out.

Three: bring taste. This is the hardest one to hand over. Looking at something that technically works and saying, no, that's not it. Pushing back. Cutting scope. Saying no when it isn't right. The AI will happily build anything you ask for. It has no sense of when to stop. You do.

[pause] Later on I'll show you a video of me fixing a small issue from start to finish. Watch for all three jobs in there. Where I decide what matters, where I instruct, and where I push back. [click]

slides.theme: Reusable setups, with project memory walked through in detail.
slides.script:
Those were things to build. These are ways to set up the work. Recipes you can reuse every week.

I'll walk through one: project memory. It's a plain text file of rules that every AI session reads first. My conventions, how I like things done, what never to touch. So I don't have to explain myself every single morning.

The trick is keeping it short. I have one rule for that file: if removing a line wouldn't change the AI's behaviour, it's gone. No essays, no nice-to-knows. Every line has to earn its spot.

And one rule inside it that matters most: before anything gets built, we agree on a pass or fail check. A test, a command, something that says yes or no. That one line has saved me more time than any fancy tool.

For the power users: one line in my memory file says the AI may not touch a shared online database until I say a magic word. A small script also stops it and asks me. And no, I'm not telling you the word.

The others on the board, the parallel posse, spec first, the morning brief, are all worth a try. [click]

slides.theme: MCP: one standard plug that lets the AI use other tools and data, like a USB-C port for AI apps.
slides.script:
One more piece of setup. A lot of what I need lives outside my code. That's what MCP is for. Model Context Protocol. It's an open standard for connecting AI apps to other systems. Files, databases, search, design tools like Figma. The people behind it put it like this: think of it as a USB-C port for AI apps. One plug, lots of things fit.

A small connector program, called a server, sits in front of a tool and offers actions and data. Your AI app, like Claude Code, plugs into it.

An everyday example. Someone hands you a design in Figma. Plug in a Figma server, and the AI can look at the design itself, instead of you describing it.

For the power users: my AI's long-term memory is a folder of plain Obsidian notes, about three hundred of them. It writes everything it researches there, and searches it through its own MCP server. I even draw agent workflows as boxes and arrows, and it walks the drawing. [click]

slides.theme: Three simple steps to get going.
slides.script:
So how do you actually start? Three steps.

One: start small. One tool, one real task. Not a toy example, something you actually need done this week. Nothing fancy. Writing a test, cleaning up some messy code, drafting the intro doc for a project.

Two: feel it out. Try things. Notice what works and what doesn't. Adjust. You'll learn more from one real task than from ten tutorials.

Three: grow confidence. As you start trusting it on small things, take on bigger problems. Trust gets built the same way it does with a new colleague. A little at a time. And you'll find your own limits for what you hand over.

And when you ask it to do something, ask well. [click]

slides.theme: What is an LLM? Appendix TLDR plus link.
slides.script:
A large language model is trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next piece of text, again and again. It reads and writes in tokens: small chunks of words. The context window is its working memory. Underneath, it's a big file of numbers (the parameters) plus a small program that runs them.

Read more: https://erikpantzar.github.io/misc/work-in-progress/reading.html#llm

slides.theme: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus and Fable: how models differ and how to pick. Appendix TLDR plus link.
slides.script:
Claude comes in tiers: Haiku is fastest and cheapest, Sonnet balances speed and intelligence, Opus is for long agentic coding and hard work, and Fable sits above it for the hardest reasoning. They also differ in speed, price per token and context window. Start with Opus for most work, or start cheap with Haiku and move up when tests show you need to. Compare models on your own tasks.

Read more: https://erikpantzar.github.io/misc/work-in-progress/reading.html#models
